findings.text: The retro's experiment review is a regular checkpoint, but by the text's account a fixed-interval schedule alone gives the least effective results and quick extinction (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2; Ch 7.3); recognition tied to completed actions (a ratio basis) holds action-completion norms better, since "the performance-contingent (or ratio) reward schedules generally lead to better performance than the time-contingent (or interval) schedules" [V] (Ch 4.2).
findings.problem: 'holds action-completion norms better' is set against fixed-interval 'quick extinction', so it reads as extinction resistance. Table 4.2 gives fixed ratio quick extinction too; only the variable schedules give slow extinction. The Hamner [V] backs better performance, not durability. Also 'least effective results' drops the source's 'In most situations' (the hedged [V] sits earlier in the same paragraph).
findings.evidence: source 5297-5300 (Table 4.2): Fixed ratio 'Leads quickly to very high and stable performance' | 'Quick extinction of behavior'; Variable interval and Variable ratio 'Slow extinction of behavior'. Source 5369-5370: ratio schedules 'generally lead to better performance'. Source 10400: 'In most situations the fixed-interval schedule produces the least effective results'.
findings.fix: correct: The retro's experiment review is a regular checkpoint, but by the text's account a fixed-interval schedule alone gives quick extinction (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2) and in most situations the least effective results (Ch 7.3); recognition tied to completed actions (a ratio basis) lifts follow-through, since "the performance-contingent (or ratio) reward schedules generally lead to better performance than the time-contingent (or interval) schedules" [V] (Ch 4.2), and only the variable schedules give slow extinction (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2).
